hypothesis: Achieving 80%+ CI pass rate on first-run AI output requires internal sandbox CI loops where the system detects failures and applies auto-fixes iteratively before the final PR is submitted.

findings.claim: SWE-agent (Princeton NLP) uses a ReAct loop with a specialized Agent-Computer Interface, achieving 18.29% resolve rate on full SWE-bench with GPT-4 in early 2024. The loop repeats up to 30+ steps, capturing stack traces and refining edits until tests pass or the turn limit is reached.

By 2025, agentic harnesses combined with higher-reasoning models (Claude 3.5/4) reached 40-50%+ on SWE-bench full, with top multi-agent teams reaching 77-79% on the human-verified SWE-bench Verified subset.

OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin) resolves approximately 53% of SWE-bench Verified issues using Claude 3.5 Sonnet with a specialized CodeAct v2 environment for terminal commands and file management. Approximately 20% of its own repository commits are agent-authored.

Aider uses an Architect/Editor pattern where a high-reasoning model plans fixes and a faster model applies diffs. It automatically runs linters and test suites after every edit, retrying up to 6 times on failure. Achieved 88% on its Polyglot benchmark and 26.3% on SWE-bench Lite in mid-2024.

Devin (Cognition Labs) uses a dual-agent architecture: a Coding Agent implements while a separate Review Agent (Bug Catcher) acts as skeptic, forcing repair loops before code reaches the terminal. Integrates with CI/CD and Sentry for automatic Diagnosis-Remediation-Validation cycles. Reported 13.86% on SWE-bench at March 2024 launch.

ReVeal (Microsoft Research Asia, June 2025) uses a Generation->Self-Verification->Tool Execution->Refinement loop with Turn-level Advantage Policy Optimization (TAPO). Key finding: a model trained on only 3 turns continues to improve over 20+ turns at inference, eventually surpassing much larger models like DeepSeek-R1.

The foundational iterative self-repair architecture has four components: Generator (produces code), Executor (sandboxed runtime), Critic/Reflector (analyzes failures via LLM), and Episodic Memory (stores failed attempts to prevent repetition). Established by Self-Debug (2023), Reflexion (2023), and LEVER (2023).
Self-Debug (2023) formalized the 'rubber duck debugging' loop for LLMs, showing that requiring a model to explain its code line-by-line before fixing it significantly improves repair success rates.
Reflexion (2023) introduced 'verbal reinforcement learning' where agents maintain persistent linguistic memory of mistakes to guide future actions, enabling cross-task learning from failures.

LDB - Large Language Model Debugger (2024) uses a 'segmentation' approach where the agent breaks code into small blocks and verifies intermediate variable states of each block, mimicking a human developer using a debugger watch window.

Modern pre-PR validation uses a four-layer architecture: (1) deterministic static analysis with LLM-hallucination-specific rulesets, (2) semantic/requirement alignment checking against Jira/Linear tickets, (3) dynamic runtime verification in sandboxed Micro-VMs (E2B), (4) agentic critique via LLM-as-Judge using a higher-reasoning model.

Multi-agent orchestration for code repair uses specialized sub-agents: Diagnoser (repo navigation), Planner (managerial coordination), Engineer (implementation), and Validator (sandboxed testing). The Validator runs the full CI/CD suite and provides healing instructions back to the Engineer if regressions are detected.
Accenture reported an 84% increase in successful builds when using AI coding agents (GitHub Copilot integration) to catch syntax and logic errors before CI pipeline execution.

Nubank reported 12x efficiency improvement in engineering hours and 20x cost savings during a massive ETL migration using Devin agents to handle repetitive refactoring tasks with autonomous CI fix loops.

CodeRabbit employs a two-stage agentic loop: stage 1 gathers deep context using AST-based Codegraph and Model Context Protocol (MCP), stage 2 uses a reasoning agent to filter false positives and enforce natural language quality gates.
Predictive test selection using AI semantic analysis of code changes can reduce feedback loop duration by 50-70% while maintaining safety, enabling faster iteration cycles for self-healing agents.

Spec-Driven Development (SDD) pattern: agents generate specification documents and acceptance tests BEFORE implementation. The PR gate only opens if the agent provides logs proving those specific tests passed in a sandbox.

LEVER (2023) proposes a specialized verifier model trained to score the likelihood that a program is correct based on the combination of prompt, code, and execution result -- separating verification from generation.

key_insights: Self-healing loops follow a consistent four-component architecture (Generator, Executor, Critic, Episodic Memory) that has evolved from academic papers (2023) to production systems (2025), with the critical shift being from 'LLM-as-Judge' to 'Environment-as-Judge' where sandboxed runtimes provide objective pass/fail signals.

Iteration count matters more than model size: ReVeal showed a model trained on 3 turns can surpass larger models when given 20+ inference turns, and Aider's 6-retry loop with an Architect/Editor split achieves 88% on polyglot benchmarks -- the self-healing loop itself is the primary quality driver.

SWE-bench resolve rates jumped from ~18% (single-agent, 2024) to 53-79% (multi-agent orchestration, 2025-2026) by combining specialized sub-agents (Diagnoser, Planner, Engineer, Validator) with sandboxed CI execution, validating the hypothesis that internal sandbox CI loops are necessary for high pass rates.
gaps: No reliable data on optimal iteration cap -- when do self-healing loops hit diminishing returns? ReVeal mentions 20+ turns but no systematic study of cost-vs-quality tradeoff curves across iteration counts.
Missing comparison of sandbox CI loop overhead (compute cost, wall-clock time) versus the quality gains -- no published cost-benefit analysis for running 6-30 iterations before PR submission.
No independent benchmarks for commercial tools (Devin, CodeRabbit) -- all performance claims come from vendor marketing; SWE-bench entries from commercial agents lack full reproducibility details.

Limited research on failure modes of self-healing loops -- when agents get stuck in infinite repair cycles, oscillate between fixes, or degrade code quality through accumulated patches across iterations.
No data on how self-healing loop effectiveness varies by language, framework, or codebase complexity -- all major benchmarks focus on Python repositories.
